segments: This is article 6 in the KVM virtualization series, focusing on declarative configuration and troubleshooting with NixOS as a KVM host. For general concepts (how QEMU/KVM work, libvirt architecture, and virt-manager usage), first read the general installation guide.
1. An overview of KVM configuration on NixOS
1.1 Why NixOS is particularly well suited to KVM
NixOS’s declarative configuration model is an excellent fit for KVM virtualization, particularly in four areas:
Advantage
Description
Complete configuration in one file

Kernel modules, libvirtd, QEMU, virt-manager, networking, and the firewall are all brought together in one configuration.nix or flake, rather than scattered across /etc/libvirt/, /etc/modprobe.d/, hand-written systemd units, and other locations
Reproducibility

When moving to a new machine, reinstalling, or deploying to multiple hosts, pin nixpkgs and module inputs and account for host hardware/network differences; restore VM disks, libvirt runtime state, NVRAM, and TPM state separately
Declarative VM definitions
With the community project NixVirt, you can even define virtual machines declaratively in Nix syntax (a Nix representation of domain XML), achieving "VM as Code"
Atomic upgrades and rollbacks

If VMs encounter problems after a kernel / QEMU / libvirt upgrade, select the previous configuration generation in the bootloader to roll back; this does not roll back external state in VM disks, NVRAM, or TPMs

After applying the configuration, log in again for group membership to take effect, then check the libvirt URI, KVM, and networking. No rebuild or VM execution was performed for this article.

libvirtd.enable = true automatically brings in the QEMU/KVM userspace components, so there is no need to declare pkgs.qemu_kvm separately. If you need a particular QEMU version or additional QEMU functionality (such as virtiofsd), specify it explicitly through qemu.package and qemu.vhostUserPackages.
2. Declarative configuration in detail

The following is a complete KVM host configuration for the NixOS configuration model, using the nixos-unstable module checked for this article as an interface snapshot (real projects should follow the nixpkgs pinned by flake.lock). It is grouped by function, with explanations for each group.
2.1 Kernel modules and boot parameters
What each parameter does:
kvm-amd: the kernel module for AMD-V hardware virtualization. After loading it, check with lsmod | grep kvm; you should see kvm_amd and kvm.

iommu.strict=1: controls synchronous invalidation on DMA unmap; it is not a switch for enabling AMD IOMMU. On AMD, firmware and the kernel usually initialize it automatically; verify IOMMU groups, interrupt remapping, and VFIO. SVM is the CPU virtualization switch, while AMD-Vi is the IOMMU feature.
iommu=pt: can change the default DMA domain for host devices; it cannot be claimed to always improve performance. It also changes the isolation boundary, so choose according to your threat model.
nested=1: allows use of svm instructions inside a VM, enabling nested virtualization.

Check whether IOMMU is active with dmesg | grep -i iommu; you should see AMD-Vi: Interrupt remapping enabled or similar output. Check IOMMU grouping with find /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/ -type l | sort -V.

2.3 GUI and client tools

The win-virtio package provides virtio-win.iso; its actual path depends on the installation profile and package layout. For systemPackages, locate it under /run/current-system/sw/share/ or in the current store package, rather than assuming it is in the user profile. When creating a Windows VM, mount this ISO as a second CDROM to load virtio storage and network drivers during installation.
2.4 Firewall configuration

Do not treat trustedInterfaces = [ "virbr0" ] as a default requirement; it broadens guests’ inbound access to host services. First inspect the libvirt network’s nftables/iptables rules and the NixOS firewall, then allow only the services actually needed, such as DHCP/DNS. For example, where genuinely necessary:
This is an example for inbound DNS/DHCP traffic, not a universal fix for every forwarding/NAT issue; verify traffic against the actual backend and rules.
3. Network configuration
3.1 Automatically activating the default NAT network

The default network’s existence, active state, and autostart state are libvirt runtime state. This interface snapshot copies the package’s default network definition on initial setup while preserving an existing file. You must still explicitly inspect net-list --all, net-info default, and subnet conflicts. For an existing persistent network, you can set net-autostart default as an authorized administrative action; this does not give Nix declarative ownership of all domain/network state.

If a service is genuinely needed to activate an existing network, the example below first checks whether it is active to avoid a duplicate net-start. It does not run net-destroy when the service stops, so rebuilds/restarts do not interrupt guest networking.

If the project switches to modular daemons, dependencies must match the actual services; do not claim that both monolithic and modular daemons are enabled by default. If fully declarative network XML is required, evaluate NixVirt and explicitly define the scope of its takeover of existing resources.
3.2 Bridged networking (Bridged Mode)
To connect VMs directly to the host’s physical network, with IP addresses on the same network as the host, use bridged mode instead of the default NAT:
Then use virsh net-define to create a libvirt network pointing to br0, or select "Bridge device" for the VM’s network interface in virt-manager and enter br0.

In bridged mode, the host no longer controls the physical interface’s IP configuration directly (the IP moves to br0). Do not make this change directly on a machine connected over remote SSH: a configuration error can disconnect you. Validate it locally first.

4. dconf configuration: eliminating initial connection delays

Presetting the URI/autoconnect settings can reduce manual connection steps, but cannot guarantee the elimination of all startup delays. NixOS dconf profiles, Home Manager dconf.settings, and GUI user state have different precedence. Do not accidentally lock settings when you only intend to set defaults. Enabling lockAll below restricts user overrides; choose according to your needs.

Some users find that virt-manager’s interface remains stuck on a spinning "Connecting..." message at first startup. The reason is that virt-manager has no preset libvirt connection URI and requires qemu:///system to be entered manually before it can connect.
Pre-populating the autoconnect configuration through dconf can resolve this:

programs.dconf.profiles is a NixOS system-module interface; Home Manager uses dconf.settings to write user configuration. Their scope and precedence differ, so a system profile should not be described as Home Manager-style. Preset these settings only when an actual connection-configuration problem occurs; do not infer a fault merely from Wayland or the packaging method. A Home Manager example:
5. AMD GPU passthrough and display options
5.1 Host capability checklist

The configuration depends on device capabilities rather than a particular machine model. First record CPU virtualization support, firmware AMD-Vi/IOMMU support, the kernel driver, IOMMU groups, independently resettable GPU/audio functions, and an alternative display or out-of-band management path.
Capability
What to check
AMD-V/SVM; nested environments also require the host to expose it
Target device functions and driver, ROM, and reset support
Kernel driver
The common AMD graphics driver is amdgpu
AMD-Vi, interrupt remapping, and actual group isolation
Recovery
An independent display/control path and a working boot generation
5.2 Basic IOMMU and VFIO configuration
Obtain the PCI device’s vendor:device ID:

Use the placeholders <GPU_VENDOR_DEVICE_ID> and <GPU_AUDIO_VENDOR_DEVICE_ID>; do not copy someone else’s IDs. ID matching may include multiple devices of the same model. Where necessary, design binding around the BDF and driver_override.
5.3 The AMD GPU reset bug and vendor-reset
Some AMD GPUs, especially dGPUs and less often iGPUs, have a "reset bug": the GPU cannot be cleanly reset after the VM shuts down, causing errors or a lockup on the VM’s second start.
An option to consider only for supported devices: check vendor-reset’s device support list and kernel compatibility before deciding to load it:

vendor-reset supports only specific device and kernel combinations. If a reset failure occurs, check the project’s support list first. Do not assume that a “newer GPU” is automatically supported, or that the module is guaranteed to fix reset failures.
5.4 Single-GPU passthrough (the specialisation approach)

This section is an illustrative boot configuration that requires separate validation. Binding the only GPU or blacklisting amdgpu may remove all local display output from the host. Prepare a verified recovery generation and an independent management path in advance. video=efifb:off does not guarantee coverage of modern simpledrm/firmware framebuffers; device reset and rebinding to the host must also be tested. Check specialisation merge semantics and the actual kernelParams before building.

If you want to pass an iGPU through to a Windows VM for gaming and accept that the NixOS host loses its display during passthrough, use NixOS’s specialisation feature to create a "VFIO mode" boot entry:

After rebooting, an additional "VFIO" option appears in the systemd-boot menu; select it to enter VFIO passthrough mode. A regular generation can serve as a recovery option, but external disk/firmware state does not automatically roll back with a generation.
5.5 virtio-gpu + virgl (an alternative for 3D acceleration)

If you do not want full GPU passthrough but still need 3D acceleration in a Linux guest, use virtio-gpu with virgl (OpenGL). Vulkan/Venus is a separate version/configuration path that requires its own validation:

virtio-gpu/virgl and QXL/SPICE use different display paths. Validate suitability and performance against the guest desktop, drivers, GL support, and actual workload.
6. Common NixOS issues and troubleshooting
6.1 Troubleshooting quick reference
Problem
Symptoms
Solution
Group membership has not taken effect
Confirm extraGroups = ["libvirtd"], then log out and log back in (not newgrp)
The default network is inactive
virsh net-list returns no output / "network 'default' is not active"
Add the systemd oneshot service from Section 3.1
virt-manager is stuck connecting
The interface keeps showing a spinning "Connecting..." message
Add the dconf autoconnect configuration from Section 4
OVMF firmware cannot be found
Ensure libvirtd.enable = true (OVMF is included automatically); for older VMs, remove the <loader> and <nvram> tags
Poor QEMU graphics performance
The VM interface stutters and the mouse drifts
Use lsmod | grep kvm to confirm that kvm_amd is loaded; use virtio drivers in the VM; on Wayland, try GDK_BACKEND=x11 virt-manager
Nested virtualization is unavailable
lsmod | grep kvm produces no output inside the VM
Add boot.extraModprobeConfig = "options kvm_amd nested=1" and reboot
The KVM module is not loaded
Confirm that SVM Mode (AMD) / VT-x (Intel) is enabled in BIOS/UEFI
SPICE rendering issues on Wayland
Window flickering and input lag
Try GDK_BACKEND=x11 virt-manager, or switch the VM to QXL Video + an X11 guest in virt-manager
USB redirection does not work
No USB devices appear in the SPICE menu
Confirm virtualisation.spiceUSBRedirection.enable = true; confirm that the user has spice-gtk installed
The GPU cannot be released after the VM shuts down
The GPU-passthrough VM reports an error on its second start
Check reset logs, device support, and whether vendor-reset applies (Section 5.3)
6.2 Diagnostic command quick reference
6.3 Special considerations for Wayland hosts
When running virt-manager and SPICE clients on a Wayland host, validate each combination against the versions of the compositor, client, guest agent, and guest desktop:

Starting virt-manager: if a missing GTK theme prevents startup, set the cursor theme through Home Manager:
home.pointerCursor = {
  gtk.enable = true;
  package = pkgs.vanilla-dmz;
  name = "Vanilla-DMZ";
};

SPICE client performance: distinguish client rendering, guest driver, and remote bandwidth issues first. Evaluate virtio-gpu/virgl for supported local combinations; SPICE GL generally requires a local Unix socket

Clipboard sharing: integration depends on protocol support in the guest agent and compositor. Test host and guest sessions separately; do not classify every Wayland combination as unsupported or assume switching to X11 will fix every problem
7. Relationship to the NixOS VM build system
This section discusses two complementary but non-overlapping NixOS virtualization capabilities:
Aspect
KVM host (this article)
NixOS VM builds
Role
A hypervisor for running general-purpose VMs (Linux/Windows/macOS)
Use Nix expressions to declaratively build NixOS VM images
Configuration method
nixos-build-vm or nix-build '<nixpkgs/nixos>' -A vm
Typical uses
Running Windows games / testing other distributions / multi-tenant isolation
Testing NixOS configurations in CI, building cloud images, and quickly validating Nix expressions
Output
Disk images (qcow2/raw) + libvirt domain XML
A directly executable result/bin/run-*-vm launch script

How they complement each other On the KVM host configured in this article, you can run NixOS VM images built with nixos-build-vm. Both use the same qemu_kvm backend; only their management and build approaches differ. For details, see the NixOS Virtualization and Deployment MOC.
